summary: Year 2 pupils (ages 6-7) recognise, find, name, and write the fractions 1/3, 1/4, 2/4, and 3/4 of a length, shape, set of objects, or quantity. Two linked ideas mature: the DENOMINATOR says how many EQUAL parts (or equal groups) to share the whole into, and the NUMERATOR says how many of those parts to take, so a non-unit fraction like 3/4 is three of the quarter-parts, not a single piece. Work moves between continuous wholes (shading part of a rectangle or marking a length) and discrete sets (a third of 12 counters), always keeping the whole explicit and fixed.
misconceptions: Reading the denominator as the group SIZE, not the number of groups (1/3 of 12 -> makes groups of 3)
Treating a non-unit fraction like a unit fraction - taking only ONE part for 3/4
Number-vs-quantity: sharing an equal COUNT of unequal-sized items rather than equal amount
Losing track of the whole, or ignoring leftover items when a set doesn't divide evenly

activities.title: Fraction-of-a-set bench: share into equal groups, then take some
steps: Put out 12 counters as the whole. To find 1/3, share ALL 12 into 3 equal groups (one group per hoop) and take one group - record '1/3 of 12 = 4'.
To find 3/4, share all 12 into 4 equal groups (3 in each) and take THREE of the four groups - record '3/4 of 12 = 9'.
Say aloud 'the bottom number is how many equal groups; the top number is how many groups I take' as you act it out.
Re-show the same fraction as a shaded strip or rectangle divided into the denominator and shaded to the numerator, to see the continuous and discrete versions side by side.

Check a non-dividing case: with a different set of items that does not share evenly (for example 10 counters into 3 groups), notice the leftover. It means the groups cannot all be equal with whole items, so that fraction of the set cannot be found exactly with whole counters (1/3 of 10 is not 3).
activities.insight: The denominator sets how many EQUAL groups/parts to make; the numerator says how many of those to take - so 3/4 is three quarters, not one piece, and the same fraction describes both a set and a shape.

activities.title: Build a non-unit fraction from unit-fraction parts
steps: Find a unit fraction first: share the whole into denominator-many equal parts and take one (e.g. 1/4 of a strip, or 1/4 of 12 counters = 3).
Build 3/4 by repeating that quarter three times (1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4), counting the quarters taken.
State the link: 3/4 means three of the four equal parts, so it is three unit-fractions put together.
Write the fraction next to the action each time so the notation stays tied to the meaning.
activities.insight: A non-unit fraction is repeated unit fractions: 3/4 is three quarters, built by taking one quarter three times.

activities.title: Same number or same amount? Guarding against the count-vs-quantity trap
steps: Compare a third of 12 LARGE counters with a third of 12 TINY counters: is the NUMBER of things the same? Is the total AMOUNT the same?

With a mixed set of big and small pieces of the same stuff (e.g. pieces of food to share fairly), check whether equal-COUNT groups also hold an equal AMOUNT. When the whole is an amount of stuff, amount, not count, is what fair sharing must make equal. Exact equal amounts may not be possible without cutting pieces.
Discuss aloud: 'same number of things, or same amount?' to separate the two ideas.
activities.insight: When the whole is an amount of stuff, fair sharing means giving each share an equal AMOUNT. With identical counters, counting gives equal amounts, but with unequal-sized pieces an equal count is NOT the same as an equal amount, so children must check the amount, not just the number of things. When the question is about the number of objects in a set, the count is what matters.

activities.title: Fraction of a length on a number line or ruler
steps: Mark a length or strip into denominator-many equal parts and find 1/4 of it.
Compare this with 1/4 of a set of counters: how are the two alike (share into 4 equal parts, take one) and unlike (a length is continuous; counters are separate things)?
Find 2/4 and 3/4 of the same length and notice 2/4 is halfway and 3/4 is three of the four equal parts.
activities.insight: The same share-then-take rule applies to lengths as to sets and shapes, so fractions transfer across continuous and discrete wholes.

activities.title: Naming and writing practice (recognition and recall check)
steps: Match fractions (1/3, 1/4, 2/4, 3/4) to correctly shaded pictures of shapes and sets.
Complete statements such as '3/4 of 12 = __' and '1/3 of 12 = __'.
Spot and reject a tempting wrong answer such as '1/3 of 12 is 3' (which reads the denominator as a group size).
activities.insight: Fractions of amounts can be named, matched, and written once their meaning is secure, consolidating the link between notation and quantity.

checkQuestion: Put out 12 counters. Ask: 'Find one-third of these counters, then find three-quarters of these counters, and tell me how you worked out each one.' Then ask: 'Why do you share by the bottom number, and what does the top number tell you to do?'
checkAnswer: One-third of 12: share into 3 equal groups (4 in each) -> 4. Three-quarters of 12: share into 4 equal groups (3 in each) and take 3 groups -> 9. The bottom number (denominator) says how many equal groups/parts to make; the top number (numerator) says how many of those parts to take.
